title: Combination Vehicles
summary: How to drive, brake, turn, couple, uncouple and inspect a tractor-trailer safely.

blocks.text: More than half of truck driver deaths in crashes come from rollovers. A fully loaded rig is 10 times more likely to roll over in a crash than an empty one, because its center of gravity is higher.

items: Keep cargo as low as possible, centered and spread out. A load shifted to one side makes the trailer lean and a rollover more likely.
Drive slowly around corners, on-ramps and off-ramps. Rollovers happen when you turn too fast.
Steer gently and smoothly. A sudden steering move can tip a trailer over.
Avoid quick lane changes.

blocks.text: In a quick lane change, rearward amplification causes the crack-the-whip effect: the steering move grows larger toward the back of the rig. The rear trailer is the most likely to turn over, sometimes without the tractor tipping.

rows: Rearward amplification 2.0
The rear trailer is twice as likely to turn over as the tractor
Triples: 3.5
The last trailer rolls 3.5 times as easily as a five-axle tractor

blocks.text: Keep at least 1 second for each 10 feet of length, plus 1 second above 40 mph. A 60-foot rig at 50 mph needs 6 + 1 = 7 seconds.

items: A large combination takes longer to stop empty than fully loaded. When lightly loaded, stiff springs and strong brakes give poor traction, so the wheels lock easily.
A bobtail tractor (no trailer) can be very hard to stop smoothly and takes longer to stop than a fully loaded tractor-semitrailer.
When trailer wheels lock, the trailer tends to swing around. This trailer jackknife is more likely when the trailer is empty or lightly loaded.
The earliest and best way to spot a trailer skid is in your mirrors. Check them whenever you brake hard.

If the trailer skids, release the brakes to get traction back. Don't use the trailer hand brake to straighten the rig; the trailer brakes caused the skid. Once the wheels grip, the trailer will follow the tractor.
Low-slung units (lowboys, car carriers, moving vans, possum-belly livestock trailers) can get stuck on raised crossings.
So can a single-axle tractor pulling a long trailer whose landing gear is set for a tandem-axle tractor.
If you get stuck on the tracks, get out and away from them first, then call for help.

blocks.text: In a turn, the rear wheels follow a different path than the front. This is off-tracking, or cheating. Longer rigs off-track more, and with more than one trailer, the rear wheels of the last trailer off-track the most.

items: If you can't turn right without entering another lane, turn wide as you finish the turn. Swinging left before the turn invites drivers to pass on your right.
Keep the rear close to the curb (without running over it) so no one can squeeze by on the right.
Back in a straight line when you can. If you must curve, back toward the driver's side so you can see.
To start, turn the steering wheel opposite to the way you want the trailer to go.
Once the trailer starts to turn, turn the wheel the other way to follow it.
If the trailer drifts off your path, correct by turning the top of the wheel toward the drift.
Back slowly, check both mirrors often, use pull-ups, and get out to re-check your path if unsure.

rows: Trailer hand valve
Also called the trolley valve or Johnson bar. Use it only to test trailer brakes, never while driving (skid risk) and never to park (air can leak away).
Tractor protection valve
Keeps air in the tractor if the trailer breaks away or leaks badly. Closes automatically at 20 to 45 psi, venting the trailer emergency line so the trailer emergency brakes come on.
Trailer air supply control
Red, eight-sided knob. Push in to supply air to the trailer; pull out to shut air off and set the trailer emergency brakes.
Service line
Also called the control or signal line. Carries air from the foot brake or trailer hand brake to relay valves, which apply trailer brakes quickly. Often coded blue.
Emergency line
Also called the supply line. Fills the trailer tanks and controls the emergency brakes. Losing its pressure sets the trailer emergency brakes. Often coded red.
Glad hands
Couplers for the two air lines. Clean the couplers and seals, press the seals together at 90 degrees, then turn to lock.
Dummy couplers
Hold unused hoses so water and dirt stay out of the lines
Shut-off valves
Also called cut-out cocks. Open on every trailer that tows another; closed only at the back of the last trailer.

items: If a trailer breaks loose and tears the emergency line, the trailer emergency brakes come on and the tractor protection valve closes (the air supply knob pops out).
A major service line leak may go unnoticed until you brake. Then tank pressure drops fast, and if it gets low enough the trailer emergency brakes come on.

Crossed air lines on a trailer with spring brakes: the springs won't release. On an older trailer without spring brakes, you could drive off with no trailer brakes at all. Always test the trailer brakes first.
Drain trailer tanks every day. Even with automatic drains, open them to make sure moisture is out.
Converter dollies and trailers built before 1975 don't need spring brakes. Their emergency brakes hold only while tank air lasts, so always chock them when parked.
Trailers and converter dollies built on or after March 1, 1998 must have ABS.
Trailer-only ABS: if the tractor starts to jackknife or you lose steering, let up on the brakes (if safe) until you regain control.
ABS never lets you drive faster, follow closer or drive less carefully. Brake as you always have.

Inspect the fifth wheel: secure, undamaged, and greased (no grease means friction and steering problems). It should tilt down toward the rear, with jaws open and the safety unlocking handle in the automatic lock position.
Check the area, chock the trailer wheels or make sure its spring brakes are on, and check that any cargo is secured.
Line the tractor up directly in front of the trailer. Backing under at an angle can push the trailer sideways and break the landing gear.
Back slowly until the fifth wheel just touches the trailer, then set the parking brake and shift to neutral.
Check trailer height: low enough that the tractor lifts it slightly. Too high and it may not couple; too low and you can hit the trailer nose.
Connect the emergency and service air lines and support them so they won't be crushed.
Push in the air supply knob and wait for normal pressure. Shut off the engine so you can hear the trailer brakes apply and release.
Pull out the air supply knob to lock the trailer brakes.
Back under the trailer slowly in the lowest reverse gear until the kingpin locks.
Tug test: raise the landing gear slightly off the ground and pull gently forward with the trailer brakes still locked.
Set the parking brake, shift to neutral, shut off the engine and take the key so no one moves the truck while you are under it.
Inspect the coupling: no space between upper and lower fifth wheel, jaws closed around the shank of the kingpin (not the head), locking lever locked, safety latch in place.
Plug in the electrical cord, and check that lines are undamaged and clear of moving parts.
Raise the landing gear, starting in low range and switching to high once it's free of weight. Raise it all the way and secure the crank handle.
Remove and store the wheel chocks.

blocks.text: A gap between the fifth wheel plates means the kingpin may be sitting on top of closed jaws, and the trailer could come loose. If the coupling isn't right, don't drive it. Get it fixed.

Gooseneck hitch: open the clamp latch and lube the ball, lower the coupler over the ball and latch the clamp, attach the safety chains, connect the light wiring and check all lights, then lower and stow the jacks.

items: Park on ground that can hold the trailer, with the tractor lined up straight.
Pull out the air supply knob to lock the trailer brakes. Back up gently to ease pressure on the locking jaws, and set the parking brake while pushing against the kingpin.
Chock the trailer wheels if it has no spring brakes, or if you aren't sure.
Lower the landing gear to firm contact. If loaded, give the crank a few extra turns in low gear to take some weight off the tractor (don't lift the trailer off the fifth wheel).
Disconnect the air lines (store them on dummy couplers) and hang the electrical cable plug-down to keep moisture out.
Pull the release handle to open, keeping your legs and feet clear of the rear tractor wheels.
Pull forward until the fifth wheel clears, but stop with the tractor frame still under the trailer in case the landing gear sinks or collapses.
Set the brake, check that the ground and landing gear are holding, then drive clear.
Lower fifth wheel: securely mounted, greased, no visible gap, jaws around the kingpin shank, release arm seated, safety latch engaged.
Air lines: properly connected to the glad hands, no leaks, no damage, and enough slack for turns.
Landing gear: fully raised, not bent or damaged, crank handle secured. Never drive with it part way up; it can catch on railroad tracks.

rows: Air flow to all trailers

Push in the air supply knob and apply the hand brake. At the back of the last trailer, open the emergency line valve and listen for air, then the service line. Close both. No air? Make sure all trailer and dolly shut-off valves are open.
Tractor protection valve
With the system charged, shut off the engine and fan the brake pedal. The air supply knob should pop out at the maker's setting, usually 20 to 45 psi.
Trailer emergency brakes
Check that the trailer rolls freely, then pull out the air supply knob and gently pull against the trailer. It should hold.
Trailer service brakes
With normal pressure and parking brakes released, roll forward slowly and apply the trailer hand control. You should feel the brakes.

blocks.text: If the tractor protection valve doesn't work, a leak in a hose or trailer brake can drain all the tractor's air and set the emergency brakes, with possible loss of control.

keyPoints: Keep cargo low and centered, and take turns and ramps slowly to prevent rollovers.
Steer gently: the crack-the-whip effect makes the last trailer the most likely to tip.
An empty rig or a bobtail takes longer to stop than a loaded rig.
If the trailer skids, release the brakes; never use the hand valve to straighten it or to park.
The tractor protection valve closes at 20 to 45 psi; the red eight-sided knob controls trailer air.
Emergency (supply) line fills tanks and controls emergency brakes; the service line carries brake signals.
After coupling, there must be no gap and the jaws must close around the kingpin shank.
Raise the landing gear all the way, and stop with the frame under the trailer when uncoupling.
